title: STOMATIN-DEFICIENT CRYOHYDROCYTOSIS WITH NEUROLOGIC DEFECTS
alt_titles: GLUT1 DEFICIENCY SYNDROME WITH PSEUDOHYPERKALEMIA AND HEMOLYSIS
CRYOHYDROCYTOSIS, STOMATIN-DEFICIENT, WITH MENTAL RETARDATION, SEIZURES, CATARACTS, AND MASSIVE HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects (SDCHCN) is caused by mutation in the SLC2A1 gene (138140), which encodes the GLUT1 glucose transporter, on chromosome 1p34.2.

checks.evidence_quote: We now show that sdCHC is associated with mutations in SLC2A1 that cause both loss of glucose transport and a cation leak
checks.explanation: Title and abstract state sdCHC results from SLC2A1 mutations; the cases show neurologic features.

checks.claim: The SLC2A1 gene encodes the GLUT1 glucose transporter.
checks.evidence_quote: Glucose transporter 1 (glut1) deficiency syndromes (glut1DSs) result from mutations in SLC2A1, encoding glut1.
checks.explanation: States SLC2A1 encodes GLUT1.

checks.claim: The SLC2A1 gene is located on chromosome 1p34.2.
checks.evidence_quote: Glucose transporter 1 (glut1) deficiency syndromes (glut1DSs) result from mutations in SLC2A1, encoding glut1.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not give the chromosomal location, but your rules count standard location notes as supported.

paragraphs.text: Stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects is a rare disorder. Fricke et al. (2004) knew of only 2 cases. Flatt et al. (2011) described it as a form of stomatocytosis that is also a form of GLUT1 deficiency syndrome. The red cells are stomatocytic and deficient in stomatin (Flatt et al., 2011). They leak sodium and potassium, and they are extremely leaky at 0 degrees C, which gives the phenotype known as cryohydrocytosis (Fricke et al., 2004). Bawazir et al. (2012) showed that the leak causes hemolysis and causes pseudohyperkalemia, a falsely high potassium level in stored blood samples. The 2 patients reported by Fricke et al. (2004) had a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts, and massive hepatosplenomegaly.

paragraphs.text: Fricke et al. (2004) reported new cases of stomatin-deficient hereditary stomatocytosis. Two patients had stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis. Both showed a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts, and massive hepatosplenomegaly. Their red cells showed pronounced cation leaks at 37 degrees C, with markedly abnormal intracellular sodium and potassium concentrations. The leak was at its lowest at around 20 to 25 degrees C, so the cells were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C. The red cells were deficient in stomatin, but immunocytochemistry showed that the deficiency was not complete.

checks.explanation: Stated directly.

paragraphs.text: Flatt et al. (2011) proposed that certain SLC2A1 mutations turn GLUT1 into a transporter that leaks cations, as shown by expression studies in Xenopus oocytes. They noted that GLUT1 is the main glucose transporter in the mammalian blood-brain barrier and that GLUT1 deficiency syndromes cause an array of neurologic symptoms.

checks.explanation: The mutant GLUT1 leaks cations, as shown in oocytes.
